contracts.name: UniswapV2Pair
contracts.purpose: A Uniswap V2 constant-product AMM pair holding reserves of two ERC20 tokens. It lets users add liquidity (mint LP tokens), remove liquidity (burn LP tokens), and swap one token for the other with a 0.3% fee. It also maintains cumulative price oracle accumulators and optionally mints a protocol fee share to the factory's feeTo address.

threats.title: Manipulate reserves during swap
threats.target: After a swap, the fee-adjusted product k never decreases.
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit a flash-swap callback to manipulate the reserves by executing a swap that results in a negative k product, potentially draining liquidity before the invariant check occurs.

threats.title: Bypass liquidity checks
threats.target: mint and burn require nonzero liquidity minted or nonzero amounts of both tokens returned respectively.
threats.approach: An attacker could create a malicious contract that calls mint with zero liquidity or calls burn with zero amounts of both tokens, bypassing the checks and manipulating the LP token supply.

threats.title: Exploit price accumulator updates
threats.target: The price accumulators are updated only when timeElapsed > 0 and both reserves are nonzero.
threats.approach: An attacker could manipulate the timing of swaps to ensure that the price accumulators are not updated correctly, leading to inaccurate price information and potential profit from arbitrage.

threats.title: Drain excess balances
threats.target: Calls skim(to) to send the excess of balances over reserves to an arbitrary address.
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit the skim function by calling it repeatedly to drain excess tokens from the contract, especially if they can manipulate the reserves through swaps.

threats.title: Reset kLast improperly
threats.target: kLast is nonzero only when the fee is on, and is reset to 0 by _mintFee when the fee is off.
threats.approach: An attacker could manipulate the minting process to reset kLast improperly, allowing them to exploit the fee structure and gain an unfair advantage in liquidity provision.

threats.title: Reentrancy through external calls
threats.target: The lock modifier makes mint, burn, swap, skim and sync non-reentrant.
threats.approach: An attacker could create a malicious contract that calls the swap function, triggering a reentrant call before the lock is enforced, allowing them to manipulate reserves or drain liquidity.

threats.title: Manipulate blockTimestampLast
threats.target: After mint, burn, swap and sync, reserve0 and reserve1 equal the pair's actual token balances.
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit the timing of transactions to manipulate blockTimestampLast, affecting the price calculations and potentially leading to profit from swaps.

threats.title: Unauthorized access to feeTo
threats.target: feeTo receives minted LP tokens as the protocol fee.
threats.approach: An attacker could exploit the feeTo mechanism by manipulating the factory's feeTo address, redirecting fees to an unauthorized address.

health.headline: Nothing critical, and 3 medium severity issues worth a look.

findings.title: Block Timestamp Dependency
findings.description: Block timestamps can be manipulated by miners within a short range
findings.fix: Avoid using timestamps for critical logic or accept ~15 second variance

findings.title: Missing SPDX License Identifier
findings.description: All source files should specify a license
findings.fix: Add // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT at the top of the file

findings.title: 9 storage slots serialise this contract
findings.description: Every write to these forces the entrypoints touching them into a queue on Monad: unlocked, reserve0, reserve1, blockTimestampLast, price0CumulativeLast, price1CumulativeLast, token0, token1, kLast.
findings.fix: Key the state by the caller where the value is theirs, or split a shared counter into stripes that sum back.

findings.title: Give 'unlocked' a key
findings.description: 'unlocked' is one slot written by mint, burn, swap, skim and sync, and it blocks 15 entrypoint pairs. If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is. Up to 15 fewer blocked pairs
findings.fix:
mapping(address => uint) public unlocked;

unlocked[msg.sender] = newValue;

findings.title: Give 'reserve0' a key
findings.description: 'reserve0' is one slot written by mint, burn, swap and sync, and it blocks 14 entrypoint pairs. If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is. Up to 14 fewer blocked pairs
findings.fix:

reserve0[msg.sender] = newValue;

findings.title: Give 'reserve1' a key
findings.description: 'reserve1' is one slot written by mint, burn, swap and sync, and it blocks 14 entrypoint pairs. If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is. Up to 14 fewer blocked pairs

reserve1[msg.sender] = newValue;

findings.title: Give 'blockTimestampLast' a key
findings.description: 'blockTimestampLast' is one slot written by mint, burn, swap and sync, and it blocks 10 entrypoint pairs. If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is. Up to 10 fewer blocked pairs
findings.fix:
mapping(address => uint32) public blockTimestampLast;

blockTimestampLast[msg.sender] = newValue;

findings.title: Shard the counter 'price0CumulativeLast'
findings.description: mint, burn, swap and sync all increment 'price0CumulativeLast', a single slot. Splitting it across N stripes lets N transactions proceed at once; the true value is the sum, read only where it is actually needed. Up to 10 fewer blocked pairs

findings.title: Pack the small state variables together
findings.description: factory, token0, token1 and blockTimestampLast are each narrower than a word. Declared next to each other they share one slot, which is both cheaper to write and one conflict point instead of several. Fewer slots written, ~2,100 gas saved per slot removed

findings.title: 10 functions have no gas bound
findings.description: solc could not bound these, so their cost depends on a loop whose length is decided at runtime and a caller can push them past the block gas limit: burn, mint, name, permit, skim, swap, symbol, sync, transfer, transferFrom.
findings.fix: Bound the loops, or let callers process a range they choose so the work per transaction is theirs to cap.

findings.title: Gas variance costs real money on Monad
findings.description: Monad debits the sender for the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so anything a wallet pads onto the estimate is spent. solc cannot bound burn(address), mint(address), name() and 7 more, which is where wallets fall back to a large default limit. Affects monad. Unbounded functions: 10.
findings.fix: Bound the loops, and have your frontend set an explicit gas limit for operations whose cost is fixed rather than letting the wallet estimate and pad.

findings.title: Storage is spread too thinly to amortise Monad's page charge
findings.description: 6 slots across 2 pages. Monad pays 8,100 gas for the first touch of each 128-slot page, so slots that sit alone on a page cost more than they would on a per-slot schedule. Summed over the 3 calls traced, that is +700 gas. Affects monad. Storage delta: +700 gas.
findings.fix: Group state that is read together into a struct so it lands on one page. Each mapping key gets its own page, but a struct stored under that key shares it.

findings.title: State contention will serialise this contract
findings.description: 4 of 10 entrypoints can run concurrently, grade D. 21 of 55 entrypoint pairs always collide, and 12 more collide when they touch the same key, on unlocked, reserve0, reserve1. This only converts into throughput on a chain that executes transactions in parallel. Monad does; every other chain in this comparison executes sequentially, so the same layout buys nothing there and costs nothing either. Affects monad. Colliding entrypoint pairs: 21 of 55.
findings.fix: Key hot state by sender or by id instead of writing to one shared slot. The Parallel Profiler lists the exact pairs and the variables behind them.

findings.title: How long before your app can say the transaction is done
findings.description: Monad reaches deterministic finality in 600 ms, two consensus slots. Base and Arbitrum One confirm through a single sequencer within a couple of seconds, but that confirmation is a promise from the operator; irreversible settlement waits on Ethereum, and a withdrawal waits seven days. Ethereum itself takes about 12.8 minutes. Which number matters depends on what the user is allowed to do next. Affects base, arbitrum. Monad hard finality: 600 ms.

findings.title: Rollups charge for calldata on top of execution gas
findings.description: Base, Arbitrum One publish every transaction's calldata to Ethereum and bill for it separately, and the figures here are execution gas only. The traced calls carry a median of 68 bytes each. Measured against those chains' own fee oracles the omitted charge is fractions of a cent even for a 39 KB deployment, since EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free, so it is a real gap rather than a large one. It moves with Ethereum's fee market, not with your contract. Affects base, arbitrum. Median calldata: 68 B.

findings.title: Monad has no global mempool
findings.description: Transactions are forwarded to the next few block leaders rather than gossiped network-wide, so anything that watches pending transactions works differently. This contract does not appear to depend on pending-transaction visibility, so it is context rather than a change. Affects monad.

data.headline: 0% of concurrent transaction pairs run without contention. 0 of 6 entrypoints stay parallel.
data.summary: Almost every transaction against this contract has to wait for the one before it. 9 slots are shared by every caller: unlocked, reserve0, reserve1 and blockTimestampLast, and others. chains.name: Monad
caveats: Gas is charged on the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so a padded limit is money spent.
Cold account access costs 10,100 gas against 2,600 elsewhere, which makes call-heavy contracts use more gas units.
There is no global mempool. Transactions are forwarded to the next few leaders instead.
EIP-4844 blob transactions are not supported.
Full nodes do not serve arbitrary historical state, so some indexing patterns need an archive provider.
EIP-7702 delegated accounts cannot be taken below 10 MON and cannot use CREATE or CREATE2.
The ecosystem is younger than the established L2s, so fewer battle-tested integrations exist.

chains.name: Ethereum
caveats: The most expensive execution environment of the group by a wide margin.
Two epochs, roughly 12.8 minutes, before a block is economically final.
24 KB contract size limit forces large systems into proxies or diamonds.

chains.name: Base
caveats: A single sequencer orders every transaction, so liveness depends on one operator.
Each transaction pays an L1 data fee on top of execution gas, which dominates for calldata-heavy calls.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Arbitrum One
caveats: `block.number` returns an L1 block number, which breaks contracts that assume L2 block cadence.
Transactions pay an L1 data component that is often larger than execution gas.
A single sequencer orders every transaction.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Polygon PoS
caveats: Security comes from its own validator set rather than from Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.
Historically prone to reorgs of several blocks under load.

chains.name: BNB Smart Chain
caveats: A small validator set relative to Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

health.headline: Nothing critical, and 3 medium severity issues worth a look.

contracts.purpose: A Uniswap V2 liquidity pair: a constant-product automated market maker for two ERC20 tokens. It tracks reserves, issues LP tokens (which it also implements via UniswapV2ERC20) for deposits, redeems them for pro-rata token amounts, executes swaps with a 0.3% fee, optionally mints a protocol fee share to a feeTo address, and maintains cumulative price accumulators for TWAP oracles.

threats.title: Flash-swap callback manipulates oracle and external protocols
threats.target: Price accumulators / reserves invariant
threats.approach: Attacker calls swap with non-empty data. In uniswapV2Call, with tokens optimistically sent out and reserves not yet updated, they interact with third-party protocols that read getReserves or spot balances. Those protocols see a distorted price, and the attacker profits before repaying. The pair's k check passes because repayment is made in the same transaction.

threats.title: Single-block price manipulation to skew TWAP
threats.target: Price cumulative accumulators
threats.approach: Attacker swaps to move the price at the end of a block (or sandwiches the first transaction in a block), so the next update writes price*timeElapsed using the manipulated reserves. Over a short TWAP window, or with low liquidity, this shifts the oracle average. They then exploit a lending or derivative protocol that consumes the TWAP and swap back, paying only the 0.3% fee.

threats.title: First-depositor share inflation / donation attack
threats.target: LP supply and MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY
threats.approach: Attacker is the first minter and deposits a tiny amount, so liquidity is just above MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY. They then donate large token amounts directly to the pair and call sync to inflate the reserves per LP unit. Later depositors' proportional min(amount0*supply/reserve0, amount1*supply/reserve1) rounds down, and they receive few or zero LP (mint reverts only if exactly 0). The attacker redeems and captures the rounding loss.

threats.title: Front-running mint with skewed ratio
threats.target: Minted LP equals min of proportional shares
threats.approach: The LP transfers tokens to the pair and calls mint in a separate step. A searcher sees this in the mempool and swaps to skew the ratio first, or calls skim/sync. The min() formula then credits the LP only for the scarcer side, so the excess value stays in the pool and is captured by existing LPs or the attacker's later burn.

threats.title: Stealing deposited tokens between transfer and mint/burn
threats.target: Pair token balances / LP tokens held by pair
threats.approach: When a user's tokens are sent to the pair before mint, anyone can call mint(attacker) first and receive the LP tokens, because mint reads balance minus reserve. Likewise, LP tokens sent to the pair before burn can be burned by any caller with the attacker as `to`. skim(attacker) can also take excess tokens. This affects non-atomic integrators that do not bundle the steps in one transaction.

threats.title: Fee-on-transfer or rebasing token breaks accounting
threats.target: Reserves vs balances invariant and the swap k check
threats.approach: A pool created with a deflationary, rebasing or hook-bearing token makes the balance received differ from the amount sent, or makes balances change without a pair call. An attacker uses skim to pull positive rebases or sync to lock in reduced reserves. Reserves diverge from true balances, and other LPs are diluted or the pair's price is distorted.

threats.title: Malicious or non-standard token behaviour in transfers and balanceOf
threats.target: Token balances / reentrancy lock
threats.approach: A token in the pair is attacker-controlled. Its transfer or balanceOf can re-enter other contracts (such as the router or integrator protocols that read getReserves, which has no lock), return manipulated balances so the k check passes, or return false/no data in a way that _safeTransfer tolerates. This drains the honest token side of the pool, or exploits read-only reentrancy on stale reserves.

threats.title: uint112 overflow lock-up / reserve update failure
threats.target: Reserves fit in uint112
threats.approach: An attacker donates or swaps in huge amounts of a high-supply token so balance exceeds uint112. All mint, burn, swap and sync calls then revert on the overflow require. The pool is frozen, and liquidity is locked unless balances are reduced via skim, which may itself be blocked by the token.

threats.title: Protocol fee dilution or kLast manipulation
threats.target: kLast and feeTo LP minting
threats.approach: Attacker times mint and burn around fee-on transitions. When feeTo is switched on or off, kLast is stale or reset to 0. Using donations plus sync, or the sqrt(k) growth calculation, they inflate rootK so that the feeTo recipient receives a skewed LP mint. This dilutes LPs, or lets the attacker avoid fee accrual by entering and exiting around the fee-minting step.

threats.title: Rounding and dust-based pool draining via tiny swaps or burns
threats.target: Constant-product invariant / burn amounts
threats.approach: With very low liquidity or tokens with few decimals, attacker repeatedly executes swaps whose fee rounding (integer division with *1000 and *3 terms) or burns that round down favour them. This extracts dust each time. At scale this erodes LP value, particularly in pools reduced to near MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY.

threats.title: Initialize hijack on pair deployed outside factory
threats.target: token0/token1 set once by factory
threats.approach: If the pair is deployed with a non-factory deployer, or the factory address is misconfigured, an attacker calls initialize with malicious tokens before the legitimate setup. The pair's pooled assets are then defined by the attacker, and users interacting with the known pair address are drained.

threats.title: Callback abuse via swap data and to address
threats.target: Swap recipient restrictions / invariant
threats.approach: The attacker uses a `to` contract that, in uniswapV2Call, manipulates the token balances seen by the final balanceOf check, for example by sending in a different asset that the token wraps or by interacting with a token whose balanceOf is affected by external state. This passes the k check without a real repayment of equivalent value. The `to != token0/token1` check is the only guard.

findings.title: Block Timestamp Dependency
findings.description: Block timestamps can be manipulated by miners within a short range
findings.fix: Avoid using timestamps for critical logic or accept ~15 second variance
Key the state by the caller where the value is theirs, or split a shared counter into stripes that sum back.
findings.title: 9 storage slots serialise this contract
findings.description: Every write to these forces the entrypoints touching them into a queue on Monad: unlocked, reserve0, reserve1, blockTimestampLast, price0CumulativeLast, price1CumulativeLast, token0, token1, kLast.

findings.fix:
mapping(address => uint) public unlocked;

unlocked[msg.sender] = newValue;
findings.title: Give 'unlocked' a key
findings.description: 'unlocked' is one slot written by mint, burn, swap, skim and sync, and it blocks 15 entrypoint pairs. If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is. Up to 15 fewer blocked pairs

If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is. Up to 10 fewer blocked pairs

findings.title: Shard the counter 'price0CumulativeLast'
findings.description: mint, burn, swap and sync all increment 'price0CumulativeLast', a single slot. Splitting it across N stripes lets N transactions proceed at once; the true value is the sum, read only where it is actually needed. Up to 10 fewer blocked pairs

findings.title: Pack the small state variables together
findings.description: factory, token0, token1 and blockTimestampLast are each narrower than a word. Declared next to each other they share one slot, which is both cheaper to write and one conflict point instead of several. Fewer slots written, ~2,100 gas saved per slot removed

findings.fix: Bound the loops, or let callers process a range they choose so the work per transaction is theirs to cap.
findings.title: 10 functions have no gas bound
findings.description: solc could not bound these, so their cost depends on a loop whose length is decided at runtime and a caller can push them past the block gas limit: burn, mint, name, permit, skim, swap, symbol, sync, transfer, transferFrom.

findings.fix: Bound the loops, and have your frontend set an explicit gas limit for operations whose cost is fixed rather than letting the wallet estimate and pad.
findings.title: Gas variance costs real money on Monad
findings.description: Monad debits the sender for the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so anything a wallet pads onto the estimate is spent. solc cannot bound burn(address), mint(address), name() and 7 more, which is where wallets fall back to a large default limit. Affects monad. Unbounded functions: 10.

findings.fix: Group state that is read together into a struct so it lands on one page. Each mapping key gets its own page, but a struct stored under that key shares it.
findings.title: Storage is spread too thinly to amortise Monad's page charge
findings.description: 6 slots across 2 pages. Monad pays 8,100 gas for the first touch of each 128-slot page, so slots that sit alone on a page cost more than they would on a per-slot schedule. Summed over the 3 calls traced, that is +700 gas. Affects monad. Storage delta: +700 gas.

findings.fix: Key hot state by sender or by id instead of writing to one shared slot. The Parallel Profiler lists the exact pairs and the variables behind them.
findings.title: State contention will serialise this contract
findings.description: 4 of 10 entrypoints can run concurrently, grade D. 21 of 55 entrypoint pairs always collide, and 12 more collide when they touch the same key, on unlocked, reserve0, reserve1. This only converts into throughput on a chain that executes transactions in parallel. Monad does; every other chain in this comparison executes sequentially, so the same layout buys nothing there and costs nothing either. Affects monad. Colliding entrypoint pairs: 21 of 55.

findings.title: How long before your app can say the transaction is done
findings.description: Monad reaches deterministic finality in 600 ms, two consensus slots. Base and Arbitrum One confirm through a single sequencer within a couple of seconds, but that confirmation is a promise from the operator; irreversible settlement waits on Ethereum, and a withdrawal waits seven days. Ethereum itself takes about 12.8 minutes. Which number matters depends on what the user is allowed to do next. Affects base, arbitrum. Monad hard finality: 600 ms.

findings.title: Rollups charge for calldata on top of execution gas
findings.description: Base, Arbitrum One publish every transaction's calldata to Ethereum and bill for it separately, and the figures here are execution gas only. The traced calls carry a median of 68 bytes each. Measured against those chains' own fee oracles the omitted charge is fractions of a cent even for a 39 KB deployment, since EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free, so it is a real gap rather than a large one. It moves with Ethereum's fee market, not with your contract. Affects base, arbitrum. Median calldata: 68 B.

findings.title: Monad has no global mempool
findings.description: Transactions are forwarded to the next few block leaders rather than gossiped network-wide, so anything that watches pending transactions works differently. This contract does not appear to depend on pending-transaction visibility, so it is context rather than a change. Affects monad.

chains.name: Monad
caveats: Gas is charged on the transaction's gas limit, not the gas it uses, so a padded limit is money spent.
Cold account access costs 10,100 gas against 2,600 elsewhere, which makes call-heavy contracts use more gas units.
There is no global mempool. Transactions are forwarded to the next few leaders instead.
EIP-4844 blob transactions are not supported.
Full nodes do not serve arbitrary historical state, so some indexing patterns need an archive provider.
EIP-7702 delegated accounts cannot be taken below 10 MON and cannot use CREATE or CREATE2.
The ecosystem is younger than the established L2s, so fewer battle-tested integrations exist.

chains.name: Ethereum
caveats: The most expensive execution environment of the group by a wide margin.
Two epochs, roughly 12.8 minutes, before a block is economically final.
24 KB contract size limit forces large systems into proxies or diamonds.

chains.name: Base
caveats: A single sequencer orders every transaction, so liveness depends on one operator.
Each transaction pays an L1 data fee on top of execution gas, which dominates for calldata-heavy calls.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Arbitrum One
caveats: `block.number` returns an L1 block number, which breaks contracts that assume L2 block cadence.
Transactions pay an L1 data component that is often larger than execution gas.
A single sequencer orders every transaction.
Withdrawals to Ethereum sit behind a seven-day challenge window.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

chains.name: Polygon PoS
caveats: Security comes from its own validator set rather than from Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.
Historically prone to reorgs of several blocks under load.

chains.name: BNB Smart Chain
caveats: A small validator set relative to Ethereum.
Execution is sequential, so a parallel-friendly contract layout buys nothing.

Gas figures come from executing the contract in a local EVM with synthesised arguments. A function guarded by a balance or permission check will revert, and reverted calls are marked rather than counted.
Only state-changing functions are traced. View and pure functions cost nothing to call from outside a transaction.

Only execution and intrinsic gas is modelled. Rollups additionally charge for publishing calldata to Ethereum, which is not included. Measured against the live oracles, that fee is around $0.0001 on Base and $0.00002 on Arbitrum even for a 39 KB deployment, three to four orders of magnitude below the execution cost shown, because EIP-4844 blobs made data posting nearly free.
Ethereum storage cost is measured from the EVM. The Monad figure is that measurement adjusted by the published MIP-8 schedule.

parallel.summary: Part of this contract parallelises cleanly and part of it does not. 10 slots are shared by every caller: unlocked, reserve0, reserve1 and blockTimestampLast, and others. Any two transactions that touch one of them serialise. mint(), burn(), swap(), skim(), sync() and initialize() cannot run alongside each other. 17 view functions were excluded: they send no transactions and never contend.

suggestions.description: 'reserve1' is one slot written by mint, burn, swap and sync, and it blocks 14 entrypoint pairs. If its value is really per account, per market or per position, storing it under that key removes the contention rather than reducing it. If it is a genuine contract-wide invariant such as an AMM reserve or a reentrancy flag, it cannot be split and should stay as it is.

suggestions.title: Shard the counter 'price0CumulativeLast'
suggestions.description: mint, burn, swap and sync all increment 'price0CumulativeLast', a single slot. Splitting it across N stripes lets N transactions proceed at once; the true value is the sum, read only where it is actually needed.

suggestions.title: Pack the small state variables together
suggestions.impact: Fewer slots written, ~2,100 gas saved per slot removed
suggestions.description: factory, token0, token1 and blockTimestampLast are each narrower than a word. Declared next to each other they share one slot, which is both cheaper to write and one conflict point instead of several.

issues.title: Block Timestamp Dependency
issues.description: Block timestamps can be manipulated by miners within a short range
issues.recommendation: Avoid using timestamps for critical logic or accept ~15 second variance
